Group Facilitators
As Release and Reclaim grows, we’re excited to bring in additional Helping Professionals to facilitate conference calls.
Christine Chenitz has a master’s degree in Social Work and currently has a psychotherapy practice where she works with those who have experienced trauma of various types including religious and spiritual trauma and adverse religious experiences. Christine was raised in a strict form of conservative christianity within an insular community structure and has lived experience with religious trauma. In her 20s, she deconverted from christianity and began a journey of discovery. Her own struggles encouraged her to help those who have had negative experiences in religion. As she furthered her research and understanding of the experiences of religious trauma, Christine stumbled upon Marlene’s articles on Religious Trauma Syndrome and immediately felt seen. From there Christine joined Marlene’s Helping Professionals Group and joined Journey Free to further support folks recovering from adverse religious experiences. She moderates the groups, Making Connections/Friends and Dealing with Believers And The Church.
Janice Selbie was born and raised in a Canadian evangelical Christian home with parents who believed the Bible was literal and inerrant. She married a man who became a pastor and they were married for nearly 20 years, raising two daughters. In her late 30s, Janice experienced a series of tragedies which caused her sufficient doubt in the God of the bible that it shook her loose from her cognitive dissonance and prompted her to start researching other religions and exploring all that she had denied herself. After her divorce, she went back to school to become a Registered Professional Counsellor. She was thrilled to discover Marlene online and attend some of her retreats in San Francisco. Interacting with others who could relate to her own painful transition out of religious life prompted Janice to develop the Divorcing Religion Workshop.

 

Coco Owen grew up in the Seventh-day Adventist Church. She left after a crisis of faith at age 21, and began a deconstruction journey that led her to pursue graduate degrees in comparative literature and clinical psychology.

She is now a licensed psychologist in Los Angeles, CA, and has an all-telehealth private practice. She has two young-adult children, loves animals, and is happy to have joined the Journey Free community. Coco moderates the “Creativity” group.

 

Kevin Davison recalls an early Southern Illinois Pentecostal church (at age 7), where he first spoke in tongues after a laying on of hands in the children’s church basement. Many memories of children’s bible stories and restrictions on music prevailed, but with a close and loving family’s support. Jesus was the beginning and the end to a very conflicting social life until graduating from CFNI in ’95 to only become a failed missionary evangelist (to Brazil), by choice. He disappointed his family to leave “God’s plan.” He chose a different career in technology and then followed a long, drawn out, but adventurous deconstruction of his faith.

With help from a beautiful community of Reclaimers—attending retreats with accompanying therapy/coaching from Marlene and this wonderful group, he’s recovering. Now, facilitating conference calls, moderating groups, and providing technical web support.

 
Chase Marks was raised as a Jehovah’s Witness and after deciding to leave the religion in his mid-20s, he faced the reality of losing his family, friends, community, world view, and sense of self. The intense confusion, fear, shame, and anger was too much for him to deal with. Not knowing he was experiencing symptoms of religious trauma and having no tools to navigate them, he was left in a very dark and lonely place. After some time, Chase found that deep down he knew there must be more to life. That’s when he began his healing journey. He began looking into religions and spiritual practices outside of Christianity. He began working with and studying under traditional healers and medicine people. Little by little, he was finding his own path and his own answers. Ultimately, Chase realized that his healing would not come from someone else’s teachings or holy books. It would come from his own experiences and his own beliefs. Now, many years later, Chase is grateful to offer his services as a religious recovery consultant to those who are facing similar challenges leaving harmful religion. Chase is a trained health and wellness coach and he facilitates the Saturday support group for Release & Reclaim. Chase also moderates two groups for Release & Reclaim – “Sex and Pleasure”, and “Death, Mortality, Fear of Hell.”

 
Moderaters
These are the people who help keep our groups safe and productive.
Jessica (Humor and Fun, Parenting) was raised as an evangelical Christian, and while would have identified as a “progressive Christian” for most of her adult life, finally left religion altogether in 2017. Jessica is a Clinical Social Worker practicing in Southeastern Pennsylvania. Her practice focuses mostly work around trauma with children and teens. She read Marlene’s book Leaving the Fold in the summer of 2021 and joined the group Journey Free to both give and receive support from people who have similar lived experiences.

Jessica lives with her three awesome kids and her husband in Southeastern, PA.

He became disenchanted with the Evangelical world view however today he still gets value in exploring different forms of Spirituality. He moderates the Spirituality board on this site and helps out with moderating other boards too. 

Tim is a retired software engineer who has run a travel agency with his wife for over 20 years. Having traveled to many countries and meeting people of different cultures has also expanded his world view.

Dr Winell writes in Leaving the Fold: “This book is not anti-God, anti-church, or anti-spirituality, but it is anti-dogma.” Tim follows this non-dogmatic approach to exploring spirituality!

More About the Group
As a virtual group, we do not have the same kind of contact as we would in person, but we try to make it as personal as possible. This is not just a discussion group or a place to rant about religion. We are devoted to healing and growth. Among the areas growth are:

Understanding clearly what you have been through, especially religious indoctrination.
Working through feelings of anxiety, depression, anger, grief, and confusion.
Reclaiming your right to think for yourself, and learning to trust yourself.
Discovering self-love and self-care.
Learning to find direction and meaning in life instead of seeking “God’s will.”
“Coming out” to others and dealing with family and friends still “in the fold.”
Addressing relationship and sexuality issues.
Rebuilding your identity, your own values & beliefs, and a more personal “spirituality.”
Accepting this world as your home and finding new friends and community.
Learning to appreciate pleasure and enjoy life here and now
As a group member, you have access to:

Transitivity:
To show that ≻ is transitive, we need to prove that for any three alternatives x, y, and z in the set X, if x ≻ y and y ≻ z, then x ≻ z.
Assume x ≻ y and y ≻ z. By definition, x ≿ y and not y ≿ x, and y ≿ z and not z ≿ y. Since ≿ is a preference relation, it is transitive. Thus, if x ≿ y and y ≿ z, then x ≿ z.

Now, we need to show that z ≿ x is false to prove that x ≻ z. If z ≿ x were true, then by transitivity (since y ≿ z and z ≿ x), we would have y ≿ x, which contradicts the initial assumption that x ≻ y. Therefore, z ≿ x is false, and x ≻ z.

Asymmetry:
To show that ≻ is asymmetric, we need to prove that for any two alternatives x and y in the set X, if x ≻ y, then it is not the case that y ≻ x.

Based on the provided privacy notice, it doesn't seem like there is any specific body or organization that your leads generation company needs to be affiliated with. However, you should ensure that your company complies with all relevant data protection laws and regulations, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) if your business operates within the European Union. It's also important to note that if you are obtaining leads from third-party sources, you should ensure that these sources are GDPR-compliant and that individuals have willingly opted in to be contacted by businesses within your group.

\*\*How to deal with third party leads?\*\*

If you are using third-party sources for your leads, it is important to ensure that the data you receive from them is GDPR compliant. Here are a few steps you can take to ensure GDPR compliance of your third-party leads:

Conduct due diligence: Before partnering with a third-party provider, it is important to conduct due diligence to ensure that they are GDPR compliant. You can do this by reviewing their privacy policy, data protection practices, and the contracts they offer.

Obtain assurances: You should obtain assurances from the third-party provider that the data they provide is GDPR compliant. This can be done by having them sign a data processing agreement (DPA) that outlines their GDPR compliance obligations.

Obtain consent: You should obtain consent from individuals before using their personal data for marketing purposes. This can be done by having the third-party provider provide you with evidence of the individual's consent or by obtaining consent directly from the individual.

Verify data accuracy: You should verify the accuracy of the data provided by the third-party provider. This can be done by cross-checking the data with publicly available information or by using a third-party data verification service.

Provide transparency: You should provide transparency to individuals about how their personal data is being used. This can be done by providing a clear and concise privacy notice that outlines the purposes for which their personal data will be used and the legal basis for doing so.

By following these steps, you can ensure that the third-party leads you receive are GDPR compliant and that you are complying with the GDPR when using their data.

\*\*What Must we adhere too?\*\*

To ensure that you keep your customer's data safe, you should adhere to the following best practices:

Obtain explicit consent: Make sure that your customers have explicitly given you permission to collect and use their personal data.

Limit data collection: Collect only the minimum amount of data necessary to provide your services. Do not collect more data than you need.

Use secure storage: Ensure that your customer's data is stored securely and encrypted where possible.

Implement access controls: Restrict access to customer data only to employees who need it to do their job.

Regularly review data: Regularly review your customer's data to make sure it's still needed and relevant.

Provide transparency: Provide your customers with clear and concise information about how you are using their data, including who you are sharing it with.

Respond to data requests: Respond to customer data requests promptly, and allow customers to update or delete their data as needed.

Train employees: Train your employees on data protection best practices, including how to identify and report data breaches.

By following these best practices, you can help ensure that your customer's data is safe and that you are in compliance with data protection laws such as GDPR.

\*\*Key Points of GDPR\*\*\*

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a regulation in EU law on data protection and privacy for all individuals within the European Union (EU) and the European Economic Area (EEA). The GDPR aims to give control back to individuals over their personal data and to simplify the regulatory environment for international business by unifying the regulation within the EU.

To achieve compliance with the GDPR, you should take the following steps:

Understand the regulation: Make sure you are familiar with the requirements of the GDPR and how they apply to your business.

Conduct a data audit: Identify what personal data you hold, where it came from, who you share it with, and how long you keep it.

Implement appropriate technical and organizational measures: This includes the security measures that you have in place to protect personal data against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure or access.

Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO): A DPO is responsible for ensuring your organization complies with the GDPR and acts as a point of contact between your organization, data subjects, and supervisory authorities.

Obtain consent: You must obtain clear and unambiguous consent from individuals to collect and process their personal data. This means that you must clearly explain why you are collecting their data, how you will use it, and for how long you will keep it.

Respond to data subject requests: Data subjects have the right to request access to their personal data, rectification, erasure, and the right to object to processing. You must respond to these requests within a reasonable time frame.

Ensure international data transfers are compliant: If you transfer personal data outside of the EU, you must ensure that the recipient country has adequate data protection measures in place.

Conduct regular training and awareness programs: Ensure that your employees are aware of the GDPR requirements and how to handle personal data appropriately.

By following these steps, you can achieve compliance with the GDPR and protect your customers' personal data.

\*\*Key requirements of GDPR\*\*

As a lead generation business, you must comply with the GDPR's requirements for collecting, storing, and processing personal data. Here are some key requirements:

Lawful basis for processing: You must have a valid legal basis for collecting and processing personal data. This could be based on the individual's consent, a contract, a legal obligation, or legitimate interests.

Transparency: You must provide individuals with clear and concise information about how their data will be used, who it will be shared with, and how long it will be kept. This information should be provided in a privacy policy and in any communication with the individual.

Data minimization: You should only collect and process the minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve your purposes.

Accuracy: You must take reasonable steps to ensure the personal data you hold is accurate and up to date.

Security: You must take appropriate measures to ensure the security of personal data, including protecting it against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage.

Rights of data subjects: Individuals have certain rights under the GDPR, including the right to access their personal data, have it rectified, erased, or restricted, and to object to its processing.

Data protection impact assessments: You may need to conduct a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) if your processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.

To achieve compliance with the GDPR, you should conduct a thorough review of your data processing activities and implement appropriate policies and procedures to ensure compliance with these requirements. You should also consider appointing a Data Protection Officer (DPO) to oversee your compliance efforts and serve as a point of contact for individuals and supervisory authorities.'

The financial argument holds no water. The Employer has said in bargaining that, over 10 years, cutting these benefits will save $20 million. A proposal to defining the correlation between endometriosis risk and gene variants through the studies of genome-wide association and exome sequencing

Endometriosis is a chronic disease which is estimated to affect 10% of women globally and often manifests as pelvic pain and/or infertility1. These symptoms result from an overgrowth of ectopic endometrial tissue2. Endometriosis is commonly misdiagnosed for several reasons, the most notable being that pelvic pain is a symptom which overlaps with other gynecological diseases, and the lack of knowledge regarding its pathogenesis3.

However, research demonstrates that endometriosis is a partly genetically inherited disease (with a heritability of ~50%)4,5 By defining the genetic profile of endometriosis, genetic screening could provide an alternative diagnosis method and eliminate unnecessary diagnostic procedures, which would facilitate patients receiving the treatment they require.

Recently, genome research tools have been developed, such as genome-wide association (GWA) studies and exome sequencing. Through GWA studies, several candidate genes associated with endometriosis risk have been discovered, which will be discussed further on in light of a systematic literature review on endometriosis GWA studies. On the other hand, exome sequencing of endometriosis has been conducted in very few studies; there are no relevant systematic literature reviews published to date. Thus, a case-control study in Greece (Matalliotakis et al, 2017)6 will be discussed to illustrate the importance of investing in exome sequencing.

In light of this research, this paper proposes a novel combined research method of GWA and exome sequencing studies, addressing the lack of multidisciplinary studies on this topic. This could contribute to identifying the endometriosis genome, which is of great significance for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis.

A systematic review of GWA-studies of endometriosis
A GWA study takes a large population of patients that share a characteristic (ie, a disease) and a population of controls that do not share this characteristic. Then, the most frequently appearing genetic risk variants in these genomes are highlighted and considered as possible contributing genes to this characteristic—in this case endometriosis risk. These highlighted genes are the candidate genes.

In 2020, Cardoso et al7 published a systematic literature review on endometriosis. The goal of this systematic review was to describe the candidate genes and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) identified thus far, and to discuss the conflicting results of these 15 studies. The results of this review pointed to 11 candidate genes or SNPs that might be associated with an increased endometriosis risk. However, the authors identified a number of confounding factors, the most notable being the overrepresentation of Caucasian patients, and the small sample sizes of many studies. Therefore, the authors emphasize the importance of conducting GWA studies on large populations of differing ethnic backgrounds to accurately identify the risk variants specific to these distinct populations.

Exome sequencing of endometriosis: a study in Greece
Similar to GWA studies, exome sequencing selects a patient population and a control group. A specific portion of DNA of these populations are sequenced, which contain the loci of the candidate genes found through GWA studies. Then, a correlation between the possible risk variants and the disease is determined. Mutations in protein-coding DNA sequences contribute to increased disease risk. Therefore, exome sequencing does not sequence the entire genome—which includes junk DNA as well—but only the exome. Therefore, exome sequencing is a cost-effective approach to genome research, which is interesting for conducting these studies in larger quantities, globally.

In a population of 166 Greek women with endometriosis and 150 controls, Matalliotakis et al (2017)6 examined three single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to determine if they were correlated with endometriosis risk. These SNPs were rs7521902, rs10859871, rs11031006 which map to the genetic loci WNT4, VEZT, and FSHB, respectively. These SNPs were selected based on a meta-analysis of GWA studies8. Their findings indicate that the allele variants located on the loci WNT4 and FSHB could be correlated with endometriosis risk. These results are promising and could extend our knowledge of endometriosis genomics. However, they may not be applicable to every population.

The importance of combining GWAS and exome sequencing, and discussing study parameters
GWA studies are a fairly novel tool to quickly identify the allele frequency in patients’ genomes to find a relatively plausible set of candidate genes, which subsequently can be examined in exome sequencing studies. However, there are underlying genetic factors that complicate the study of endometriosis genomics. For instance, epistatic reactions, where one gene variant can “overshadow” another gene, thereby rendering the causal gene unidentifiable1. This is, as of date, impossible to examine through the software used in GWA studies due to limited computational power. Thus, the use of exome sequencing to fill in these gaps of genetical information will be crucial to unravel the endometriosis genome1.

However, exome sequencing remains critically dependent on reliable GWA data. More specifically, small sample size, lack of ethnic diversity, and incomplete patient characteristics are detrimental to the proper interpretation of a GWA study1. In the study by Matalliotakis et al (2017)6, candidate genes association rates differed according to clinical disease stage. Thus, Lalami et al1 insist that classifying patients according to their clinical characteristics is a key component to improving the detection of relevant candidate genes.

The inheritable nature of endometriosis has been well established for decades. The study of genome-wide association has improved our understanding of the genetic basis of this disease. However, endometriosis is heterogeneous and complex; its genomics have yet to be extensively researched to the point where these findings can be utilized in clinical practice. The limited amount of research published to date is a testament to this. Clearly, additional exome sequencing studies are required.

Overall, researchers agree on the need to conduct GWA studies in large, ethnically diverse, and clinically well characterized patient populations.. This is expected to yield a selection of reliable candidate genes which in turn may be investigated thoroughly in smaller (familial) populations through exome sequencing. Narrowing down this selection will ensure that exome sequencing can be utilized cost-effectively, therefore more studies may be conducted. Consequently, our knowledge of its pathogenesis can be broadened. This would lead to opportunities in developing medicine for treatment and genetic screenings for diagnoses. As a result, women with endometriosis would benefit from this advancement in women’s medical health.

This is a podcast about Presidential candidates who lost. I'm David Sadzin. My credentials? I'm a loser. When I was a kid, people told me I was gifted. Destined to do great things. Nobody told me I would struggle. Financially. Emotionally. Or if they did I didn't pay attention. I mean it's one thing to hear in passing how life can sometimes suck. It's another thing to wake up to this:

[AMBIENT NOISE OF FIRE TRUCKS]

This is the sound of my home burning to the ground. Last year, I was in bed when the banging on my door started. The itching in my lungs. When I got to the street and saw the flames on my apartment building, I did what you would've done. Pulled out my phone. Pressed record. It's how we make the unreal seem more real. You know what I mean?

A few hours later I gave my name to the Red Cross. A few hours after that, I checked into a hotel. I had no idea what was going to happen next. First a pandemic, now this? But there was one thing I did know. 

By this point, this feeling... it was familiar. You see, by this point I knew that life is not a winning proposition. Whether you're a billionaire or a bum you're gonna die in the end. And along the way it's gonna be a bumpy ride. The way I see it, there's a few ways to cope with this uncomfortable reality. You can pretend everything's fine while the world burns, you can start a religion, or you can make a podcast. 

Growing up in the US, I was raised on stories about the Presidents. Abraham Lincoln. George Washington. Maybe you learned a bit more about Reagan, Eisenhower, Taft. But we never learned about the people who ran for President and lost. History is kinda picky that way. It likes winners. 

But, if you're like me, and you've lived a life of pain, rejection, and loss, you've come to wonder if there's more to learn from the losers than the winners. If you've ever had this thought, this is your podcast.

In each episode we're gonna dive deep into the life of a Presidential election loser, someone you probably heard of only in passing, or likely never heard of at all. 

The plan - and I know what you're thinking: "This loser has a plan?" - but the plan is to cover about a dozen of the most interesting losers in Season 1. My voice won't be the only one you hear. Legit historians will be guiding us. (I know. They actually answered my emails. Shocking.) Together we're gonna look at the obstacles these people faced - personal, interpersonal, political, institutional - how they didn't overcome them - and what they did with the rest of their lives. Did they win at losing or did they lose? 

And perhaps we'll come away with a lesson or two.

Hey, you and me? We've been living through a global pandemic. All of us are mourning something we lost. Whether it's a person or just the life we used to have a few years go. Some of us are taking it better than others. Instead of just taking a step back and admitting defeat, some of us would rather tear it all down. And hey, I know the feeling.

But maybe, by the end of our little podcast journey, we will have learned what most of us were never taught: how to lose.

Greenpeace has emphasized the advantages of using solar energy for domestic purposes, which enable users to generate their own electricity. Solar energy is considered democratic since it is widely popular among users, and governments should encourage its use.

The primary components of a self-consumption photovoltaic system include solar panels, an inverter, energy storage, wiring and structure, and safety devices. Solar panels are responsible for converting sunlight directly into electricity. The inverter, on the other hand, converts the direct current generated by the panels into the alternating current used in households. Energy storage is essential to ensure a constant supply of electricity when the panels do not produce enough energy. The wiring and structure of the panels must be robust and installed in a location without shade or obstacles. Other devices, such as monitors and safety controllers, are also available to provide added benefits.

By understanding these components, homeowners can install their own solar systems and generate clean energy. Solar energy has numerous benefits, such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions, lowering energy bills, and increasing energy independence. Additionally, using solar power can potentially increase the value of a home.

Governments should take an active role in promoting the use of solar energy. Policies that incentivize homeowners to install solar systems, such as tax credits or subsidies, can help accelerate the transition to clean energy. Encouraging research and development in the solar industry can also lead to more efficient and cost-effective technology.

In conclusion, solar energy for home use offers numerous benefits, and the decreasing costs of technology have made it more accessible to households. The components of a self-consumption photovoltaic system are relatively simple and easy to understand, allowing homeowners to generate clean energy and potentially save money on energy bills. Governments should promote the use of solar energy and invest in research and development to continue improving this renewable energy source.

Rewrite the following paragraph for harar city, ethiopia without changing the nomenclature without losing citation and references 

1. Introduction
Climate change is one of the most perilous environmental aspects affecting ecosystem services, environmental sustainability and daily life (Chakroborty et al., 2020; Choudhury et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020). Changes in land use/land cover (LULC) exacerbate climate alteration by decreasing biodiversity and generating the urban heat island (UHI) consequence in cities by raising the land surface temperature (LST). Changes in LULC and LST are considered among the most widespread study themes for remote sensing (RS) scholars (Al Rakib et al., 2020a; Dey et al., 2021; Kafy et al., 2021d). Investigations on LULC and LST change aid in assessing cities' ecological health and viability (Zhou et al., 2013; Siddique et al., 2020). Worldwide urbanization has become the driving force behind environmental, social-economic and demographic transformation over the last few decades (Al Rakib et al., 2020b; 2020c; Choudhury et al., 2019; Kafy et al., 2019b). As a result of urbanization, LULC categories like green cover, wetlands, water bodies, and open fields undergo rapid transformation (Ding and Shi, 2013; Faisal et al., 2021; Kafy et al., 2021a). The haphazard conversion of one LULC feature to another has a substantial influence on the native and regional environment (Al Rakib et al., 2020a; Das et al., 2020; Rousta et al., 2018). Uncontrolled rapid urban expansion and LULC transformations have the potential to alter the hydrological, thermodynamic, and radiative activities of the earth surface, thereby amplifying the effects of climate change and heatwaves. Additionally, the unmonitored alteration of LULC expands built-up areas by displacing green cover, resulting in environmental degradation via UHI effects. Rapid urbanization rises impervious layers (structures, roads, and factories, for example), resulting in massive LST increment (Hossain et al., 2020; Ramachandra et al., 2012). Increased LST also has an effect on UHI phenomena, having a significant influence on biodiversity's primary function, local and regional climate (Luck and Wu, 2002). The built-up areas have a higher concentration of UHI due to the presence of additional impermeable surfaces. UHI is a critical topic for environmental development because it consists a variety of negative consequences for urban inhabitants (Kafy et al., 2020c). UHI concepts are processed from LST estimation from freely available, easily accessible remote sensors with a higher ranged spatiotemporal resolution (Kafy et al., 2020a). Specifically, historical medium-resolution Landsat data are repeatedly used to define the LST and to characterize the UHI influence (Choudhury et al., 2019; Kafy et al., 2020c; Naim and Kafy, 2021).

Estimating cities' LULC shifting patterns has become a critical aspect in achieving sustainable environmental enhancement (Siddique et al., 2020). Due to spatiotemporal LULC variations, the pattern of spatial landscapes alters on a variety of land surfaces and thus it became critical to ascertain LULC changes at appropriate scales using accurate time-series data. Then, perceptions of its associations for the climate change in urban areas will emerge, assisting in the comprehension of the various environmental consequences (Almazroui et al., 2013; Siddique et al., 2020). Numerous mathematical indices have been used by researchers worldwide to help them better understand changes in LULC (Mishra and Prasad, 2015). The most widely used catalogue is the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) that describes the condition of vegetation using a combination of the red and near-infrared bands of the satellite images (Gascon et al., 2016). Additionally, due to the scarcity of water, the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) detect water bodies using satellite images' near-infrared (NIR) and middle infrared (MIR) bands (McFeeters, 1996). Additionally, urbanization is a significant driver of LULC change, reducing an area's vegetation cover as it is converted to built-up areas (Kafy et al., 2019a; Pu et al., 2006). To determine the congregation of built-up areas and bare lands, Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) and the Normalized Difference Bare Soil Index (NDBSI) were calculated using the red, blue, NIR, and short wave infrared (SWIR) bands (Chen et al., 2006; Kafy et al., 2019a).

However, detecting LULC and LST consequences with accessible Landsat records is simple, but predicting upcoming variations is troublesome. Markov Chain (MC), Cellular Automata (CA), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models are the most commonly used to predict LULC change (Balzter, 2000; Santé et al., 2010; Zenil, 2010). If the LULC conversion is well-known but the spatial dependence and dissemination are unavailable, the MC model is considered (Kafy et al., 2020b; Ullah et al., 2019). The CA model, which is based on a set of conversion algorithms, uses the historical circumstances of cells in an analytical zone to classify each pixel's situation in an array (Santé et al., 2010). The most substantial benefit of the CA model is dependent on the earlier configuration of variables such as distance to road and rail network, slope, and elevation, and for this reason, this model is frequently used in utility and resource research (Ménard and Marceau, 2005). To forecast LST, ANN combined with related LULC indexes such as NDVI, NDBI, NDBSI, and NDWI can effectively estimate future changes (Mushore et al., 2017; Hasanlou and Mostofi, 2015). The potential of these indexes to simulate LST was assessed using the ANN process, and the results revealed that NDBI is the most accurate LST predictor (Ullah et al., 2019). Since it reflects earlier changing patterns and uses the LULC indices to predict future scenarios, ANN method is considered as a LST predictior (Kafy et al., 2021b; Ullah et al., 2019). A lesser dataset is also a prerequisite to build the fundamental simulation process (Dhamge et al., 2012; Ullah et al., 2019). As a result, ANN is regarded as the best method for forecasting the LST consequences (Kafy et al., 2021c; Ullah et al., 2019).

Dhaka, Bangladesh's capital city, has experienced rapid urban growth since independence due to significant urban development and rural-urban migration. The increasing population pressure has accelerated unplanned expansion in this area. Methods such as CA-ANN algorithms can be helpful in identifying the short and long standing magnitudes of LULC and LST transformation in this region. It can also assist policymakers and urban planners in abating the UHI effect. Thus, this study estimates the chronological change of LULC and its impact on LST, investigates the relationship between LST under different LULC categories, and performs a correlation analysis of different land cover indices with LST for the years 2000, 2010, and 2020. This study also used CA-ANN algorithms to model the future LULC and LST scenario for Dhaka city in 2030.

Please write 600-words responding to the following prompt:

"Identify and explain how Srinivasan's 'The Right to Sex' is related to Hirsch and Khan's \_Sexual Citizens\_. The aim of this essay is to assess your ability to 'identify, analyze, [and] interpret … different points of view.'"

Here are some additional guidelines:

1. Do not simply explain two arguments. You must also identify an explicit relationship, explain why you think that relationship exists, and provide textual evidence to support that relationship.

2. Because this is a more complex argument, you should begin your essay with a short introductory paragraph that identifies the relationship you are going to defend in the rest of the essay.

3. You do not need to compare entire essays and, in fact, may not have space to do so. You can compare sub-arguments or smaller passages in two different essays.

4. You are likely to have the easiest time writing this essay if you choose two essays/arguments that defend opposing positions. For example, you might choose to compare an argument that defends jealousy as a virtue with an argument that critiques jealousy as a vice.

5. A caution: it may seem that two authors disagree about an issue (e.g., sexual exclusivity) when in fact they are drawing different kinds of conclusions that can both be true at the same time (e.g., “polyamory is not unethical” and “monogamy is valuable”). So be sure to think carefully about how the conclusions are related to one another before you say authors “disagree.”

6. You can also write about more complex relationships. Perhaps two authors do not disagree, but one argument builds on the other author’s argument. Or perhaps both arguments work together to paint a more complex picture about a single issue. You are free to write about these relationships, but you must identify them and explain them in a clear way.

7. While you do not need to summarize entire essays, you should not ignore details that are relevant to the argument you are making. For example, if you’re trying to explain how an author would respond to the claims of another author, and you ignore the paragraph where they \*directly respond\* to that argument, your essay will not be complete. If you find there are too many relevant details, consider focusing on a different relationship/comparison. I’m happy to talk with you about your choices before you begin. You can also ask your group for feedback or head to the writing center!

8. There are two common ways to structure a comparison. You can describe one argument, describe the second, and then discuss the relationship between the two. Alternatively, you can go back and forth between the arguments throughout the entire essay. You are free to take either approach, but given the length of the essay, you might save some space by diving into the comparison.

9. You do not need to limit yourself to the words the authors have written on the page. You should also ask yourself “how would this author respond to what this other author is saying?” Your answer may be something they don’t say directly. That’s OK, but you will also need to explain why you think they would respond that way, and defend your answer with evidence from the text.

Summarize this: Because atrophy of cortical neurons is believed to be a contributing factor to the development of mood and anxiety disorders (Christoffel et al., 2011, Duman and Aghajanian, 2012), we first treated cultured cortical neurons with psychedelics from a variety of structural classes (Figures 1A and S1A) and measured the resulting changes in various morphological features. Using Sholl analysis (Ristanović et al., 2006), we observed that several psychedelics increased dendritic arbor complexity comparably to ketamine, as measured by the area under the curve of the Sholl plots as well as the maximum number of crossings (Figures 1B–1E and S1B–S1E). This increase in arbor complexity appeared to result from large changes in both the number of dendritic branches and the total length of the arbors (Figures 1F, 1H, S1F, and S1H). Psychedelics had a limited effect on the number of primary dendrites and did not alter the length of the longest dendrite. Nearly all psychedelic compounds tested were capable of robustly promoting neuritogenesis, with comparable effects being produced by tryptamines (N,N-dimethyltryptamine [DMT] and psilocin), amphetamines (2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine [DOI] and MDMA), and ergolines (lysergic acid diethylamide [LSD]). As a positive control, we treated cells with 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (DHF), a psychoplastogen structurally dissimilar to classical psychedelics (Jang et al., 2010), and found that it also increased dendritic arbor complexity (Figure S2). This neurite outgrowth structural phenotype seems to only be induced by select compounds because serotonin and D-amphetamine, molecules that are chemically related to classical psychedelics and entactogens, exerted minimal to no effects on neuritogenesis (Figure S2).
To establish the relative potencies and efficacies of hallucinogens and entactogens for promoting neurite outgrowth, we conducted 8-point dose-response studies (Figure S3). We defined 100% and 0% efficacy as the maximum number of crossings induced by ketamine (10 μM) and vehicle (0.1% DMSO), respectively. We chose the 10 μM concentration of ketamine as the upper limit because this concentration of ketamine is reached in the brain following intraperitoneal administration of an antidepressant dose in rats (Yang et al., 2018). For consistency, we used this same concentration when testing the effects of psychedelics and entactogens, with DMT being the only exception. We used a maximum 90 μM concentration of DMT in our studies to more closely mimic the brain concentration of DMT in rats treated with an antidepressant dose (Cohen and Vogel, 1972, Cameron et al., 2018). In this neuritogenesis assay, ketamine’s half maximal effective concentration (EC50) value was 132 nM. Surprisingly, the majority of the psychedelics and entactogens we tested exhibited significantly greater potency than ketamine, with LSD being particularly potent (EC50 = 0.409 nM). In fact, LSD exhibited activity across 8 orders of magnitude into the low picomolar range (Figure S3).
Notably, the anti-addictive alkaloid ibogaine (Alper, 2001, Belgers et al., 2016) was the only psychedelic tested that had absolutely no effect (Figure S4). This was a surprising result because we hypothesized that ibogaine’s long-lasting anti-addictive properties might result from its psychoplastogenic properties. Previous work by He et al., 2005 clearly demonstrated that ibogaine increases the expression of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) and that this plasticity-promoting protein is critical to ibogaine’s anti-addictive mechanism of action. Because several reports have suggested that noribogaine, a metabolite of ibogaine, might actually be the active compound in vivo (Zubaran et al., 1999, Baumann et al., 2000, Baumann et al., 2001), we decided to test its ability to promote neuritogenesis in cultured cortical neurons. Gratifyingly, noribogaine robustly increased dendritic arbor complexity with an EC50 value comparable to ketamine (Figure S3), providing additional evidence suggesting that it may be the active compound in vivo.
To assess the in vivo effects of classical psychedelics on neuritogenesis, we started treating Drosophila larvae during the first instar with LSD and DOI. As observed in rodent cortical cultures, both LSD and DOI significantly increased dendritic branching of class I sensory neurons; however, they did not increase the total length of the dendritic arbors (Figures 1J–1L). Because of the striking effects of psychedelics on the structures of immature neurons, we hypothesized that they might influence neurodevelopment. To test this, we chronically treated zebrafish embryos with compounds for 6 days immediately following dechorionation and assessed gross morphological changes and behavior. We did not observe any differences in head sizes between the treatment groups, nor did we detect any statistically significant differences in activity levels (Figure S5). Next we assessed the ability of psychedelics to promote neuritogenesis in more mature neurons by starting to treat Drosophila larvae during the late second instar. Again, psychedelics increased the branching of class I neurons, although the effect was less dramatic than that observed when treatment was started during the first instar (Figure 1M–1O). Although different developmental stages might be more or less susceptible to the effects of psychedelics, it is also possible that the smaller effect size observed after administering compounds starting at the later time point was simply the result of treating the larvae for a shorter period of time. Regardless, it was quite surprising to observe compound-induced changes in neuronal structure after initiating treatment during the late second instar because class I neurons are stereotyped and typically possess relatively few higher-order branches (Grueber et al., 2002). Moreover, our results demonstrate that psychedelics can promote changes in neuronal structure across vertebrate (rats) and invertebrate (Drosophila) species, suggesting that they act through an evolutionarily conserved mechanism.

This document is intended for both the stakeholders and the developers of the system and will be proposed to the Regional Historical Society for its approval.
Scope of Project
This software system will be a Web Publishing System for a local editor of a regional historical society. This system will be designed to maximize the editor’s productivity by providing tools to assist in automating the article review and publishing process, which would otherwise have to be performed manually. By maximizing the editor’s work efficiency and production the system will meet the editor’s needs while remaining easy to understand and use.
More specifically, this system is designed to allow an editor to manage and communicate with a group of reviewers and authors to publish articles to a public website. The software will facilitate communication between authors, reviewers, and the editor via E-Mail. Preformatted reply forms are used in every stage of the articles’ progress through the system to provide a uniform review process; the location of these forms is configurable via the application’s maintenance options. The system also contains a relational database containing a list of Authors, Reviewers, and Articles.
The Web Publishing System has four active actors and one cooperating system. 
The Author, Reader, or Reviewer accesses the Online Journal through the Internet. Any Author or Reviewer communication with the system is through email. The Editor accesses the entire system directly. There is a link to the (existing) Historical Society.

The Editor believes that a society member is much more likely to be an effective reviewer and has imposed a membership requirement for a Reviewer. The HS Database fields of interest to the Web Publishing Systems are member’s name, membership (ID) number, and email address (an optional field for the HS Database).
The Assign Reviewer use case sends the Reviewer ID to the HS Database and a Boolean is returned denoting membership status. The Update Reviewer use case requests a list of member names, membership numbers and (optional) email addresses when adding a new Reviewer. It returns a Boolean for membership status when updating a Reviewer.

Among the deep generative models, variational autoencoders (VAEs) are the pioneers in generating new samples from a learned, latent space while effectively reconstructing input data. However, the original formulation requires a stochastic sampling operation, implemented via the reparameterization trick, to approximate a posterior latent distribution. In this paper, we propose a new method that inputs the complete distributions of the encoded input into the decoder, effectively optimizing the model for the entire range of data instead of discrete samples. We treat
the encoded distributions as continuous random variables and use operations defined by the algebra of random variables during decoding. Experiments on different datasets and architectures demonstrate that this modification improves VAE-based architectures’ performance. Specifically,

• Allowing real-time audio/video communication and sharing of location between the people who spot the dog and the owner could be very helpful for identification and coordinating retrieval. This allows them to directly verify and guide, rather than just relying on alerts.
• Leveraging smartphone GPS and augmented reality for navigation guidance could be useful, but the technology would need to be very reliable for this type of important, time-sensitive task. The risk of technical issues could be frustrating.
• You're right that dog owners and walkers tend to be a community-minded group, so adoption of an app like this may be stronger if it's really focused on facilitating direct communication and connection between people. 1.1.1.4 Unreliable information should be treated with caution

Some commentators support the notion that the only role of evidence law is to facilitate the use of relevant information and its rational use by the fact-finder. In other words, there should be ‘free proof’, at least in one of the senses that that term is used.16 If this approach were followed, then evidence law would be much less complicated than it is (and discussions of evidence law would focus more on the nature of rational factfinding). An example is the following provision, applicable to racketeering prosecutions in South Africa:

The court may hear evidence, including evidence with regard to hearsay, similar facts or previous convictions … notwithstanding that such evidence might otherwise be inadmissible, provided that such evidence would not render a trial unfair.17

That nation’s Constitutional Court upheld this provision under its bill of rights, observing that ‘Any judicial officer worth her salt should be perfectly placed to make the necessary value judgment.’18

However, the uniform evidence law, like the common law before it, is informed by a series of generalised value judgments about when fact-finders can—and, more importantly, cannot—be trusted to find the facts correctly. As Gageler J observes:

When acknowledgement of the inherent uncertainty of the existence of a fact that is in issue is combined with acknowledgement of the inherent subjectivity of the process of finding that fact, scope emerges within the confines of accepted legal analysis for conceiving of at least some of the rules of evidence as measures serving a function of compensating for, or mitigating difficulties faced by, a tribunal of fact attempting to weigh some types of logically probative evidence. What emerges is the potential for conceiving of the existence and application of at least some rules of evidence as methods for correcting and improving the making of judgments of fact under conditions of uncertainty within the context of an adversary system—for conceiving of rules which Dixon sardonically described as archaic rules impeding a court's knowledge of the facts, as measures, which to the contrary, might serve to align the court’s perception of what is likely to have occurred more closely with an objective (Bayesian) assessment of what probably occurred.19

This approach goes further than the other three principles discussed above, because it applies to information that clearly provides rational support for a particular conclusion but where that conclusion is nonetheless attended by significant doubt. Even putting aside its horrifying content, the tape of the victim’s emergency call may fall into this category, because of the obvious difficulties in using an audio tape of distant footsteps to determine how many people were present at a crime scene.

There are really two ways to treat unreliable evidence cautiously. The first method is to admit it, but to alert the tribunal of fact to the dangers of acting on it. The second is simply to exclude the evidence. As a general proposition, one can argue that the first of these methods provides the best way of dealing with unreliable evidence. This is because it is difficult to see how depriving the court of relevant information can possibly promote accurate fact-finding. Admitting the evidence but alerting the jury to the dangers of acting on it, on the other hand, would seem to accord both with 
the principle that relevant information should be admitted and with the principle that unreliable information should be treated with caution.|

Exclusion may, however, be justified in either of two ways. The first is to argue that a jury is simply not to be trusted with unreliable information; better to exclude it altogether than to run the risk that the jury will give it a weight that it does not deserve. Although this belief undoubtedly played a role in the development of the law of evidence, the law’s traditional mistrust about the ability of juries to accurately assess the weight that should be given to particular types of evidence is obviously difficult to reconcile with the oft-made comments about the exceptional aptitude of the lay jury for the task of fact-finding. When evaluating the law of evidence it is, therefore, important to keep in mind the following question: is the exclusion of this evidence more likely to promote or impede accurate fact-finding? An example of this vexed problem is the use of expert witnesses. For example, the prosecution in the ouija board case called a person who claimed to have expertise in interpreting the sound of footsteps. The opinion rule and its exception for specialised knowledge (discussed in Chapter 7: Opinion) grapples with the question of whether such evidence is more likely to assist the jury (with expert knowledge the jury lacks) or to impede it (by potentially exposing it to quackery).

The second justification for exclusion may be that there is some aspect of the evidence that makes it particularly difficult for anyone, including a jury, to assess objectively. For example, if a jury learns that the defendant confessed, it may be extremely difficult for the jurors to put this out of their minds, even if they also hear evidence suggesting that the confession was procured by coercion and is therefore likely to be unreliable. In other words, the mere fact that a confession was made may make it difficult for the jury to accurately weigh the evidence against the defendant.

The common feature of these justifications is their dependence on assumptions about psychology. ‘When creating a rule of evidence’, Gageler J quotes from a recent book, The Psychological Foundations of Evidence Law, ‘the rulemakers often, and unavoidably, must act as applied psychologists. The rules of evidence reflect the rulemakers’ understanding—correct or incorrect—of the psychological processes affecting witnesses and the capabilities of factfinders.’20

Q: There are 15 trees in the grove. Grove workers will plant trees in the grove today. After they are done,
there will be 21 trees. How many trees did the grove workers plant today?
A: We start with 15 trees. Later we have 21 trees. The difference must be the number of trees they planted.
So, they must have planted 21 - 15 = 6 trees. The answer is 6.

Q: If there are 3 cars in the parking lot and 2 more cars arrive, how many cars are in the parking lot?
A: There are 3 cars in the parking lot already. 2 more arrive. Now there are 3 + 2 = 5 cars. The answer is 5.

Q: Leah had 32 chocolates and her sister had 42. If they ate 35, how many pieces do they have left in total?
A: Leah had 32 chocolates and Leah’s sister had 42. That means there were originally 32 + 42 = 74
chocolates. 35 have been eaten. So in total they still have 74 - 35 = 39 chocolates. The answer is 39.

did Jason give to Denny?
A: Jason had 20 lollipops. Since he only has 12 now, he must have given the rest to Denny. The number of
lollipops he has given to Denny must have been 20 - 12 = 8 lollipops. The answer is 8.

A: There are 4 days from monday to thursday. 5 computers were added each day. That means in total 4 \* 5 =
20 computers were added. There were 9 computers in the beginning, so now there are 9 + 20 = 29 computers.
The answer is 29.

golf balls did he have at the end of wednesday?
A: Michael initially had 58 balls. He lost 23 on Tuesday, so after that he has 58 - 23 = 35 balls. On
Wednesday he lost 2 more so now he has 35 - 2 = 33 balls. The answer is 33.

- Compassion fatigue (CF) is a state of physical and mental exhaustion caused by extended exposure to the suffering of patients (Pérez-Garca et al., 2021). It is an essential issue in nursing because it can affect nurses' well-being, job performance, and quality of patient care (Peters, 2018). In nursing, nurses are supposed to care for patients while preserving their health. However, the high demands and emotional toll of nursing practice can lead to CF (Figley, 2017). Nurses and healthcare professionals in other sectors, such as social work, psychotherapy, counselling, and other caregiving professions, also experience CF (Salmond et al., 2019).
- Studies indicate that up to 80% of nurses report CF symptoms, indicating that the prevalence of CF among nurses is significant (Xie et al., 2021). The high CF symptoms have important implications for nurses' health and the quality of patient care. Nurses with CF may experience reduced empathy towards patients, which can negatively affect the quality of care provided (Anshel & Kaplowitz, 2018). In addition, nurses with CF may face elevated rates of burnout, depression, anxiety, and physical ailments (Jasper et al., 2016; Kayser-Jones et al., 2018). The negative impacts of CF can lead to poor job performance and a higher risk of turnover, which can negatively impact the healthcare system.
- CF is also a significant concern regarding nursing staff retention and turnover. Studies indicate that nurses with CF are more likely to abandon the field, resulting in a nursing shortage (Shanafelt et al., 2016). Staff retention and turnover are significant concerns because the need for nurses is rising due to an ageing population and the rise of chronic diseases. In addition, nurses with CF may suffer decreased job satisfaction and engagement, resulting in inferior patient care (Anshel & Kaplowitz, 2018).
- The emotional and physical long-term effects of CF on nurses have yet to be adequately researched. While studies have indicated that nurses with CF face high rates of burnout, depression, anxiety, and physical symptoms, little is known about CF's long-term mental and physical health effects. This knowledge gap justifies the proposed research question: What are the long-term consequences of CF on the mental and physical health of the UK nursing workforce? 
- In addition to the negative impacts on the well-being of nurses and the quality of patient care, CF can also have financial implications for healthcare organisations. Nurses with CF may require more frequent sick leave, which can lead to increased costs for the organisation. In addition, the high turnover rates of nurses with CF can increase recruitment and training expenses. By preventing and controlling CF, healthcare organisations can improve the well-being of their workforce and the quality of treatment offered and realise long-term cost savings. 
- The proposed research uses a mixed-methods??? approach to examine the long-term effects of CF on the mental and physical health of the nursing workforce in the United Kingdom. It will adhere to the National Health Service (NHS) and Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) ethical criteria (Pehlivan and Güner, 2020).
- In addition, the planned research will investigate the causes and effects of CF from the perspective of nurses to better understand the underlying variables that contribute to CF and its influence on the lives of nurses. By understanding the causes and consequences of CF, healthcare organisations and policymakers can develop more effective interventions and policies to support nurses in preventing and managing CF. The findings of this study will also benefit nurses, as it will give them a better understanding of the impact CF has on their well-being and how they can mitigate the effects.
- The proposed research will contribute to the existing literature on compassion fatigue in nursing by concentrating on CF's long-term mental and physical health effects on the UK nursing workforce. The moment Lucas entered the building, he was overwhelmed by chaos. The sounds of dozens of conversations and lockers opening and slamming shut, combined with having to maneuver through the massive crowd of students, made it hard for him to focus.
After a few seconds of staring down the crowded hallway, Lucas did manage to find some familiarity. Off in the distance, he noticed his best friend, Kevin, standing with his back to his locker. It looked like he was talking with someone whose face was obstructed by a hoodie. Lucas was eager to see his friend again, especially since he hadn’t had anyone to talk to during his suspension. 
As he began making his way towards them, Lucas realized that something was wrong. Kevin wasn’t casually leaning against his locker. He was being forcefully pinned to it by the boy in the hoodie. That’s when Lucas noticed the look of fear on his friend’s face, as the boy wasn’t talking to Kevin, he was yelling, threatening him. 
Seeing this, Lucas' excitement quickly turned to rage; his heart raced, and his casual walk became a determined run. His thoughts shifted away from his past suspension; and the argument with his dad. In this moment, the only thing that mattered was that his friend was in trouble, and no one was helping him. Brushing his way past the other students, Lucas saw that the guy who was pressing Kevin against the locker, was slightly taller and bulkier than both of them. Lucas approached from the side and greeted the boy with a hard shove. 
“Hey! Let him go, asshole!” he yelled. The push wasn’t as effective as he had hoped for, only causing the boy to stagger slightly, but as the boy turned to face him, Lucas instantly recognized him.
Lucas hesitated for a moment, surprised to see Zach in such an aggressive state. He had always known Zach to be an easygoing, friendly guy who got along with everyone. Now, his face was red with anger, and his eyes were filled with a rage that now appeared to be redirected towards Lucas. Their standoff, however, was briefly interrupted by Kevin.
“Luke? Holy shit!” He exclaimed. Lucas couldn't tell if Kevin was more excited to see him back at school after so long or if he was just happy that Lucas was helping him out of this mess. “I haven’t seen you in forever dude! Where have you be–”
“Shut the fuck up!” Zach yelled, slamming Kevin back against the locker again before turning back to face Lucas. “Stay out of this, Luke!”
Kevin, seizing the opportunity to make light of the situation, chimed in with a smirk and a joke. “You know, Zach, I think you could really use a mint. I have some in my locker. If you put me down, I can get you one.” Zach, unamused by the insult, tightened his grip on Kevin’s shoulders, causing him to wince in pain.
“You think you’re so funny, don’t you! You little punk!” Zach snarled

It seemed that Zach had a specific reason for being so angry at Kevin. Lucas had no idea what it was, but, knowing Kevin, he wasn’t very surprised. Feeling that Zach might not be entirely in the wrong. Lucas’ anger slowly dimmed. He didn’t want to fight Zach, but he still wasn’t going to let him hurt his friend.
“Wait. Zach, hold up. What’s going on?” Lucas asked calmly in an attempt to get more context and draw Zach’s focus away from Kevin. 
Zach glared at Lucas. “Your friend doesn’t know how to keep his fucking mouth shut; that’s what’s going on! Now back off, or I’ll kick both your asses.”
“Dude, c’mon,” Kevin begged, squirming against Zach’s grasp. “I didn’t say that about her. But you gotta admit, it’s kinda true.”
Zach gave Kevin a firm thump on the forehead, which inadvertently caused the back of his head to lightly bounce off of the locker. “If you say one more word, I’ll break your jaw right now!”
At this point, Kevin appeared to be bracing himself, expecting a hard punch to the face at any moment. Despite his usual efforts to deflect with humor, Lucas could see that his nerves were beginning to falter. Zach stood, staring daggers at him, fist clenched and breathing heavily. Despite his usually calm demeanor, it was clear that he was very serious, and really was prepared to fight. 
Lucas scrambled to think of a way to save his friend. He knew he couldn’t afford to get caught fighting, not on his first day back. But he was running out of time.
“Zach, listen,” he said, steadying his voice. “I get it, you’re pissed. But he’s my friend. So if you fight him, you’re gonna have to fight me too. And if we get caught; you’ll get kicked off of the football team, you’ll get stuck in detention, with Kevin, for at least a week. And I’ll probably get expelled. I don’t know what he said, but can we just drop it? Please man. Don’t do this” Zach looked to be pondering Lucas’ offer. After a brief pause, he leaned in, closer to Kevin, with one final threat.
“If I ever hear you talking shit about her again. I’m gonna beat your skinny ass, and Luke’s not gonna be able to save you. Got it!”
“Yep. Loud and clear, big guy” gulped Kevin, raising his hands in surrender. Zach, finally satisfied, released Kevin and briskly walked off, disappearing into the crowd. Lucas exhaled in relief. Kevin appeared to be mostly unharmed. Muttering “jackass,” under his breath, while straightening his shirt.
“Geez, you okay, kev?” Lucas asked, as his friend still seemed a bit shaken up.
Kevin let out a nervous laugh, trying to regain his composure. 
"Yeah, I'm good, dude. I totally had it under control." He rubbed the back of his head gingerly, wincing at the tender spot where it had connected with the locker.
“Yeah, I can tell,” Lucas said, still completely baffled by the situation. “What the hell was that all about?”
“Oh, that?” Kevin said nonchalantly. “Someone told Zach’s girlfriend that I said her face looks like melted plastic. Then she broke down crying in the middle of class. I guess she went and told him about it. What a bitch, am I right?”
 Despite the gravity of the situation, Lucas couldn't help but let out a laugh, the tension in his shoulders easing. Kevin's ability to talk himself into trouble never ceased to amaze him.
“Kevin,” he chuckled. “Did you really say that?”
“What? Me? Of course not.” Kevin replied in a sarcastic tone of voice.
“Bro, I swear, you’re gonna get us killed.” Lucas said, his laughter subsiding as he realized how bad the situation could’ve gotten.
“Hey, at least we'll have one hell of a story to tell in the afterlife, huh?,” Kevin joked, playfully nudging Lucas’s arm. “But, for real though, thanks for the save.” His expression then changed to one of curiosity. “So, where have you been, man? You totally ghosted us for, like, a month. We didn’t know if you were coming back.”
 Hearing Kevin say this made Lucas realize that his friends had no idea why he was gone for so long. His dad had only given him his phone back earlier in the morning. He didn’t bother checking, but he probably had dozens of missed calls and unread texts. Even though there was nothing he could’ve done, he still felt bad for not telling his friends what happened.

It’s hard to stand out when you have a lot of competition
But what if your business has a lot of competition?

Examples:
• Flower Delivery
• Cabinet Making
• Plumbing
• Painting
• Storage

The list goes on.

For all these businesses, customers compare their options, struggle to quickly tell the difference, and choose one at random. It’s a gamble if you get the sale.

So let’s talk about how you stand out, when you have a lot of competitors.

Here’s your first steps to stand out
3 steps to make your business stand out:
1) Group customers by their needs
2) Break those needs down to actionable parts
3) Translate the parts to what you’ll do for them
This way, you’ll be focused on customers that your competitors aren’t, or provide value to those customers in a different way.

Let’s use a real business as an example as I walk you through each step. My friend, Barrett O’Neill’s storage business, OnDemand Storage (ODS):
1) Identify customer
First, talk to your most loyal customers to see what needs they have in common.

These needs will give you an idea of what you do better than anyone else.

Steal these questions to get to know their needs:

“When using [our solution], what are you ultimately trying to get done or accomplish?”

“Are you using multiple solutions?”

“What are you trying to accomplish as you pull together multiple products and services?”

“What’s the final output you’re looking for?”

Source: Questions came from this Jobs to be Done website.

From the interviews you’ll create a list of outcomes that your customers are using your solution to achieve.

Phrase the outcomes as “I want to [do a task] so I can [achieve expected outcome]”

For a “task” include both the action the customer wants to do, and the object the customer wants to do it to.

For example:
I want to store my business equipment during the summer so I can re-open my business in the fall.

2) Understand what the customer values
Now, we want to translate these needs into something your business can act on. You want to know what your customer values and how you can solve it better than anyone.

But the word “value” is so vague.

Bain Consulting thought the word “value” was too fluffy too. So they ran a study to break value down into it’s core elements. They found 30 “Elements of Value.”

These elements are much more concrete.

Here’s why I’m so excited about this. If your customer says they want convenience what they really mean is these 4 elements:
• Simplifies
• Save time
• Avoid hassle
• Reduce effort

Those 4 elements are much easier to act on! Let’s do that in the next step.

Use the pyramid below to see what “value” really means to your customers (and check out this article if you want more of an explanation).
Bain’s Elements of Value

3) Find values where you can win / application
Now you take those elements and come up with ideas on how your business can solve them better than anyone.

Let’s take that convenience example:
• Simplifies
• Save time
• Avoid hassle
• Reduce effort

Here’s the first 3 elements as an example for OnDemand Storage (ODS):

Simplifies:
Storage is complex if the items need to be picked up from multiple locations. ODS built in-house logistic software to make the logistics simpler.

Save time:
ODS can save time during initial move-in and save time during the storage period itself. A few examples: using autopay, having the facilities ready when users arrive, movers ready on arrival.

Avoid hassle:
The big hassle for commercial storage is when they need a space too big for standard storage units, but getting their own warehouse would be too expensive.

Barrett gives businesses this mid-sized storage space so they don’t need their own warehouse. Businesses don’t need insurance, employees, or a logistics network.

You don’t need a new idea
You’ll notice that taking care of what customers value isn’t a new idea. ODS isn’t the first business to handle logistics for you.

What makes you different is that you understand what your customers value and message it to them so it’s clear you’re taking care of their specific needs.

In a later issue we’ll cover how you message your differentiation so that customers know what makes you different.

Question Title: Algorithm for ordering data so that neighbor elements are as identical as possible
Question Body:
I have a (potentially large) list `data` of 3-tuples of small non-negative integers, like
```python
data = [
 (1, 0, 5),
 (2, 4, 2),
 (3, 2, 1),
 (4, 3, 4),
 (3, 3, 1),
 (1, 2, 2),
 (4, 0, 3),
 (0, 3, 5),
 (1, 5, 1),
 (1, 5, 2),
]
```
I want to order the tuples within `data` so that neighboring tuples (`data[i]` and `data[i+1]`) are "as similar as possible".
[Define](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming\_distance) the \_dis\_similarity of two 3-tuples as the number of elements which are unequal between them. E.g.
- `(0, 1, 2)` vs. `(0, 1, 2)`: Dissimilarity `0`.
- `(0, 1, 2)` vs. `(0, 1, 3)`: Dissimilarity `1`.
- `(0, 1, 2)` vs. `(0, 2, 1)`: Dissimilarity `2`.
- `(0, 1, 2)` vs. `(3, 4, 5)`: Dissimilarity `3`.
- `(0, 1, 2)` vs. `(2, 0, 1)`: Dissimilarity `3`.

\*\*Question\*\*: What is a good algorithm for finding the ordering of `data` which minimizes the sum of dissimilarities between all neighboring 3-tuples?

### Some code
Here's a function which computes the dissimilarity between two 3-tuples:
```python
def dissimilar(t1, t2):
 return sum(int(a != b) for a, b in zip(t1, t2))
```
Here's a function which computes the summed total dissimilarity of `data`, i.e. the number which I seek to minimize:
```python
def score(data):
 return sum(dissimilar(t1, t2) for t1, t2 in zip(data, data[1:]))
```
The problem can be solved by simply running `score()` over every permutation of `data`:
```python
import itertools
n\_min = 3\*len(data) # some large number
for perm in itertools.permutations(data):
 n = score(perm)
 if n < n\_min:
 n\_min = n
 data\_sorted = list(perm)
print(data\_sorted, n\_min)
```
Though the above works, it's very slow as we explicitly check each and every permutation (resulting in O(N!) complexity). On my machine the above takes about 20 seconds when `data` has 10 elements.
For completeness, here's the result of running the above given the example `data`:
```python
data\_sorted = [
 (1, 0, 5),
 (4, 0, 3),
 (4, 3, 4),
 (0, 3, 5),
 (3, 3, 1),
 (3, 2, 1),
 (1, 5, 1),
 (1, 5, 2),
 (1, 2, 2),
 (2, 4, 2),
]
```

with `n\_min = 15`. Note that several other orderings (`10` in total) with a score of `15` exist. For my purposes these are all equivalent and I just want one of them.
### Final remarks
In practice the size of `data` may be as large as say `10000`.
The sought-after algorithm should beat O(N!), i.e. probably be polynomial in time (and space).
If no such algorithm exists, I would be interested in "near-solutions", i.e. a fast algorithm which gives an ordering of `data` with a small but not necessarily minimal total score. One such algorithm would be [lexicographic sorting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexicographic\_order), i.e.
```python
sorted(data) # score 18
```
though I hope to be able to do better than this.
### Edit (comments on accepted solution)
I have tried all of the below heuristic solutions given as code (I have not tried e.g. Google OR-tools). For large `len(data)`, I find that the solution of Andrej Kesely is both quick and gives the best results.
The idea behind this method is quite simple. The sorted list of data elements (3-tuples) is built up one by one. Given some data element, the next element is chosen to be the most similar one out of the remaining (not yet part of the sorted) data.
Essentially this solves a localized version of the problem where we only "look \_one\_ ahead", rather than optimizing globally over the entire data set. We can imagine a hierarchy of algorithms looking `n` ahead, each successively delivering better (or at least as good) results but at the cost of being much more expensive. The solution of Andrej Kesely then sits lowest in this hierarchy. The algorithm at the highest spot, looking `len(data)` ahead, solves the problem exactly.
Let's settle for "looking 1 ahead", i.e. the answer by Andrej Kesely. This leaves room for a) the choice of initial element, b) what to do when several elements are equally good candidates (same dissimilarity) for use as the next one. Choosing the first element in `data` as the initial element and the first occurrence of an element with minimal dissimilarity, both a) and b) are determined from the original order of elements within `data`. As Andrej Kesely points out, it then helps to (lex)sort `data` in advance.
In the end I went with this solution, but refined in a few ways:
- I try out the algorithm for 6 initial sortings of `data`; lex sort for columns `(0, 1, 2)`, `(2, 0, 1)`, `(1, 2, 0)`, all in ascending as well as descending order.
- For large `len(data)`, the algorithm becomes too slow for me. I suspect it scales like `O(n²)`. I thus process chunks of the data of size `n\_max` independently, with the final result being the different sorted chunks concatenated. Transitioning from one chunk to the next we expect a dissimilarity of 3, but this is unimportant if we keep `n\_max` large. I go with `n\_max = 1000`.
As an implementation note, the performance can be improved by not using `data.pop(idx)` as this itself is `O(n)`. Instead, either leave the original `data` as is and use another data structure for keeping track of which elements/indices have been used, or replace `data[idx]` with some marker value upon use.
